This paper presents DrivAerStar, a comprehensive dataset of 12,000 industrial-grade CFD simulations for vehicle aerodynamic optimization. Generated using industry-standard STAR-CCM+ software, the dataset features three rear designs parameterized by 20 CAD variables and achieves <5% error against wind tunnel validation. Benchmark results demonstrate that ML models trained on this dataset can achieve engineering accuracy while dramatically reducing computational costs.

The key strengths include: (1) providing the first publicly available, wind tunnel-validated CFD dataset meeting industrial standards; (2) employing industry-standard simulation protocols ensuring real-world relevance; (3) complete reproducibility through open data, code and documentation.

While the current geometric variations are limited to the DrivAer platform and the dataset generation required substantial computational resources (1M+ CPU core-hours), the authors have addressed these limitations by committing to expand geometric diversity and fully release all 12,000 samples. Their thorough responses during rebuttal, including adding statistical analyses and broadening ML benchmarks, further strengthen the submission.

During the discussion with the authors and reviewers, the reviewers have reached a consensus on acceptance. And finally, we request that all promised revisions and exps should be added to the camera-ready version. The dataset's unique combination of scale, fidelity, and validation makes it an exceptional contribution to both ML and engineering communities. By bridging the critical gap between academic research and industrial applications, DrivAerStar aligns perfectly with the Datasets & Benchmarks track objectives.

Dear Reviewer j6Nr, we deeply appreciate your thorough and insightful feedback across various aspects of our work, including limitations, dataset reproducibility, experimental examples, speedup comparisons, evaluation details, the role of STAR-CCM+®, and specific comments on figures and tables. Your observations are invaluable for enhancing the rigor and clarity of our manuscript, and we have carefully addressed each point as follows:

1. Regarding dataset reproducibility: Supplement dataset codes.

We thank the reviewer for pointing out the initial omission of our dataset generation code. This oversight stemmed from our adherence to double-blind review protocols, as certain implementation details required anonymization. We will promptly provide the complete anonymized codebase and migrate the full dataset—including all VTK simulation files—with step-by-step access instructions in subsequent communications, addressing storage limitations. We deeply appreciate your feedback and have formally noted these resources to be appended to our submission.

2. Regarding the application of the dataset in vehicle aerodynamic optimization: Provide specific examples to illustrate its usefulness for optimization.​


We appreciate the reviewer’s feedback highlighting the need for concrete examples of how our dataset accelerates vehicle aerodynamics optimization. Here’s a focused illustration leveraging the referenced datasets:

Consider optimizing a vehicle’s key aerodynamic features—such as rear diffuser angle, underbody design, and grille size—across different configurations. Models trained on these datasets can instantly predict aerodynamic performance (e.g., $C_D$ , lift distribution) for thousands of unseen design variants. For instance, when adjusting the rear diffuser angle within engineering ranges, a trained model avoids re-running CFD simulations that take hours to days per case (DrivAerML) , instead delivering predictions in seconds. This allows optimization algorithms to efficiently explore trade-offs—like balancing drag reduction with manufacturing feasibility or cooling efficiency—slashing the time from design concept to optimal solution from weeks to minutes. Such speed, paired with the datasets’ coverage of diverse geometries and high-fidelity flow data, directly enables rapid, data-driven aerodynamic optimization.

We will integrate this example into the revised manuscript to clarify practical utility.

3. Regarding the speedup of neural network methods: Report the speedup over state-of-the-art CFD methods for practitioners to understand its advantages.​

We appreciate the reviewer’s question regarding the speedup of neural network-based approaches over state-of-the-art CFD methods when using DrivAerStar. While direct speedup metrics for DrivAerStar-specific neural network models are not explicitly detailed in the dataset documentation, we can contextualize this based on the computational characteristics of industrial CFD simulations and typical neural network inference workflows, aligned with the dataset’s generation details:

CFD simulations for DrivAerStar, generated using industrial-grade STAR-CCM+® software, require substantial computational resources: the full dataset of 12,000 samples consumed 1,080,000 CPU core-hours across 100 computing nodes. Individual simulations, given their high-fidelity meshing (e.g., ~12 million hexahedral-dominant cells per case) and rigorous convergence criteria, would typically take hours to days to complete on parallel computing clusters.

In contrast, neural network models trained on such datasets—consistent with patterns observed in related work (e.g., DrivAerNet++ where RegDGCNN achieves inference times of ~0.85 seconds per case )—exhibit drastically reduced inference latency. Once trained, these models can predict aerodynamic quantities (e.g., drag coefficients, surface pressure distributions) in seconds, even for complex geometries.

To quantify this speedup explicitly, we will supplement the revised manuscript with direct comparisons: (1) the average wall-clock time for a single DrivAerStar CFD simulation (accounting for parallelization) and (2) the inference time of neural network models trained on DrivAerStar. This will demonstrate that neural network approaches offer speedups of several orders of magnitude, enabling rapid design iteration compared to state-of-the-art CFD.

4. Regarding the data of DrivAerNet++ and DrivAerML in Table 1: Clarify if the same evaluation method as for DrivAerStar was adopted to ensure fair comparison.​


For DrivAerNet++, all metrics in Table 1 are derived from its open - source dataset. The 8,000 samples correspond to the dataset's scale as stated in the paper. The "No" entries for PIV, Engine compartment, and Cooler reflect the dataset's content scope. The wall $y^+$ range of [50, 300] is extracted from the dataset's documentation. The average $C_D$ precision of 0.012 and wind tunnel error of ≤5.0% are calculated by us through statistical analysis of the aerodynamic coefficient data within the dataset.

For DrivAerML, the 500 samples are directly from the dataset as noted in its abstract. The "No" entries for PIV, Engine compartment, and Cooler are based on the dataset's content. Since DrivAerML does not provide wall gradient data, there is no wall $y^+$ range. The average $C_D$ precision of 0.010 and wind tunnel error of ≤6.5% are our calculations using the dataset's aerodynamic data.​

We will explicitly reference these dataset sources in Table 1's caption in the revised manuscript to enhance transparency.

5. Regarding the role of STAR-CCM+® in dataset generation: Clarify its role in dataset generation links to facilitate future extensions.​

We thank the reviewer for highlighting the need for clarity regarding STAR-CCM+® 's role in our workflow. The software was integral to both automated mesh generation and high-fidelity simulation execution. Specifically, STAR-CCM+® performed end-to-end processing: beginning with surface wrapping of morphed geometries to resolve topological imperfections, then generating optimized hexahedral-dominant volume meshes with prismatic boundary layers ($y^+ < 200$) through its production-grade algorithms, and finally solving the steady-state RANS equations with SST $k$-$\omega$ turbulence modeling. This integrated workflow was standardized across all 12,000 configurations via Java macros that maintained consistent solver settings and mesh parameters. Our forthcoming code release and step-by-step tutorials will provide complete technical specifications—including parameter sets and validation procedures—to enable straightforward reproduction and extension of DrivAerStar.

6. Regarding the underestimation of the drag coefficient by Transolver in Figure 7: Explain the reason for the underestimation.​

We thank the reviewer for this insightful observation. We hypothesize that this systematic underestimation can be attributed to the long-tailed distribution present in our dataset, as illustrated in Figure A6(b). Despite our comprehensive efforts to sample across the deformation space (see Figure A4), the distribution of $C_D$ remains skewed. This phenomenon highlights two important research directions: (1) developing neural network architectures or training pipelines that can effectively handle long-tailed CFD datasets, and (2) establishing more sophisticated methodologies for generating balanced CFD datasets. The underestimation bias likely emerges because the model is predominantly trained on more frequent, lower $C_D$ values, leading to reduced sensitivity in the high-drag regime where fewer training examples exist.

7. Regarding the improvement of prediction error with sample size in Figure 7: The current error reduction is insufficient to support the claim; supplement experiments or adjust the statement.​

We thank the reviewer for this constructive feedback. We conducted additional experiments with Transolver under the multi-vehicle setting, using 12,000 samples for training and 150 new random samples for testing—yielding more robust evaluations, with some result discrepancies from the original submission due to revised data splitting.

The key CFD metric, $C_D$ validation loss, shows consistent improvement (Table 1):

Table 1. $C_D$ validation loss under different training sample sizes in the multi-vehicle setting

| Samples | $C_D$ validation loss | Improvement |
|-|-|-|
| 400     | 0.0375 | - |
| 800     | 0.0335 | 10.67% |
| 1,200   | 0.0286 | 23.73% |
| 12,000  | 0.0266 | 29.07% |

Notably, loss decreases with larger datasets: 10.67% from 400 to 800 samples, 23.73% at 1,200, and 29.07% at 12,000. This consistent trend confirms the model scales with more data, with the 12,000-sample set delivering substantial accuracy gains critical for practical CFD.

Additionally, we compared the MAE of $C_D$ for the single-vehicle model with 400 and 4000 training samples. The MAE of $C_D$ decreases from 2.99% to 2.53%, which further demonstrates the existence of the scaling effect as the number of training samples increases.

We will refine our manuscript phrasing to better reflect these trends and update supplementary materials with new findings.

8. Regarding the appendix reference in Figure 7: Correct the reference as comprehensive scaling results are in Appendix D.2, not C.1.​

We thank the reviewer for catching this error. We will correct this in the revision.

9. Regarding Table A2: Explain the meaning of loss normalized by the initial condition.​

We thank the reviewer for this clarification request. By "normalized by the initial condition," we mean that we first compute the mean and standard deviation for each variable across the dataset, then standardize each variable using these statistics before calculating the loss, which is standard practice in CFD applications. We will clarify this normalization procedure in the revision.

We thank the reviewer for their valuable feedback. We appreciate the opportunity to clarify our decisions regarding the dataset’s creation and its scope.

1. On Computational Cost and Reproducibility

We acknowledge the significant computational investment required to generate this dataset. Our motivation for undertaking this effort and making the dataset public is to ease the burden for the broader research community. By providing this resource, we hope to enable researchers who lack access to HPC clusters and STAR-CCM+’s costly license to train and validate robust machine learning models on industrial-grade data.

2. On Generalization and the DrivAer Platform

We agree and understand the concern regarding generalization. This was a deliberate choice regarding that the DrivAer model is a widely accepted, open-source model that was specifically developed to bridge the gap between over-simplified aerodynamic vehicle models and inaccessible industry designs. It provides a foundation that is crucial for reproducible public research.

While DrivAer model does not cover all vehicle architectures, it provides a highly relevant design space for training models capable of understanding complex physical phenomena, a known challenge for models trained on less-detailed geometries. Our aim was to prioritize physical fidelity for creating surrogate models for real-world applications.

Furthermore, we view DrivAerStar as an extensible asset. We are more than willing to broaden its geometric diversity and would be happy to collaborate with industry or academic partners to generate and publish high-fidelity simulation data for new vehicle designs. This collaborative approach will allow the dataset to evolve and further enhance its value to the entire community.

We sincerely thank the reviewer for their thoughtful feedback and appreciation of the contributions and strengths of our work. Below, we address each of the stated limitations in detail:

1. Geometric Limitations

We acknowledge that no dataset can exhaustively encompass the vast design space encountered in the automotive industry.  Our choice of the DrivAer model as a foundation was deliberate, as it represents the outstanding open-source vehicle model that meets industrial-grade fidelity requirements.

While other public datasets may offer a greater number of base designs, our primary objective was to prioritize data quality and physical precision for industrial applications. To systematically address geometric variety within this high-fidelity framework, DrivAerStar was constructed with 20 carefully selected CAD parameters that span a wide and industry-relevant range of geometric features. We have also planned to incorporate additional base geometries in future work as suitable, high-quality models become available.

2. Solver Limitations

We agree that any CFD-based dataset inherits the characteristics and limitations of the solver employed. We selected STAR-CCM+ precisely because it is an industry-standard tool, extensively validated and widely adopted for external aerodynamics by leading automotive OEMs and research institutions. STAR-CCM+ is considerably more accurate and precise compared to the open-source solver OpenFOAM. Furthermore, our simulation setup and calibration protocols were developed in consultation with automotive experts, which strictly follows the industrial guidelines. While real-world deviations can never be fully eliminated, the double validation—both with trusted software and experimental configurations—ensures that DrivAerStar delivers high physical fidelity within the constraints of our computational resources.

3. Statistical Significance

We thank the reviewer for pointing out this omission in our initial submission, which was due to time constraints during the paper's preparation. If the concern refers to the experimental uncertainty of wind tunnel measurements used for CFD validation, we clarify that we only compared the error of the drag coefficient $C_D$  from wind tunnel data. We will support the complete step-by-step reproduction of this result in the soon-to-be open-sourced code, where the error range can be calculated based on cell statistics and using the open-sourced wind tunnel data.  If the concern refers to the statistical variance of machine learning experimental results, we have used more detailed plots to illustrate the error distribution, as shown in Figure 4 of the paper.

We recognize the importance of quantifying uncertainty in both contexts. We are fully committed to performing the necessary analysis and adding the appropriate error bars and a discussion of statistical significance. We believe this will substantially strengthen the paper and thank the reviewer for guiding this improvement.

summary.value:
This paper introduces DrivAerStar, a comprehensive, high-fidelity dataset for automotive aerodynamics optimization. It comprises 12,000 CFD simulations generated using the industry-standard STAR-CCM+ software, spanning variations in three basic rear designs and 20 fine-tuned CAD parameters

The paper is well-written, and significant work has been performed to demonstrate quality and utility. This work should be accepted to NeurIPS.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. Comprehensive Data Coverage: The real-world CFD dataset includes aerodynamic coefficients and detailed flowfields including surface pressures, velocity , and crucially, internal engine details with realistic airflow channels. This multi-faceted data is vital for high-fidelity ML surrogate modeling.  The significant computational resources (1,080,000 CPU core-hours, 20 TB data) underscores the scale and effort invested, lending credibility to the dataset's comprehensiveness.
2. Reproducibility: The commitment to providing reproducible workflows with scripts and validation procedures, along with open-source data processing and benchmarking code, significantly enhances the quality and utility of the dataset for the community.
3. Well-written paper with great visualizations.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
Due to page limitations, a significant portion of the ML analysis is hidden in the appendix.

If more pages are allowed in the final version, it would be good to add results beyond Transolver.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

dataset_code_comments.value: Dataset made available via hf datasets. VTK format is standard for flow physics community.

summary.value: The authors introduce DrivAerStar, a dataset containing 12,000 industry-grade vehicle CFD simulations. This dataset improves over previous vehicle CFD datasets due to (i) having more samples, (ii) using adaptive mesh strategies, (iii) using more realistic vehicle models, and (iv) using industry-grade simulation software. The authors use the DrivAerStar to train neural network surrogates for CFD, demonstrating the value of their contribution.

strengths_contributions.value:
The DrivAerStar dataset appears to be a significant improvement over previous datasets for vehicular CFD. The authors use adaptive mesh strategies, more realistic vehicle models, and industry-grade simulation software in the creation of DrivAerStar, which leads to a dataset that is closer to ground-truth CFD simulations in industry.

For the most part, the submission is well-written and easy to follow.

I appreciated that the authors provided a video in the supplementary material that summarized the contents of the dataset and their overall contribution. This video made it much easier to understand the impact of their work!

limitations_weaknesses.value:
The authors claim in the abstract that their dataset is reproducible. However, I did not see any code for generating the dataset. This claim would be better supported if the authors could provide the code for dataset generation (or at the very least, provide all the code to create the inputs to Star-CCM+).

The authors mention in the paper that their dataset could be used to accelerate vehicle aerodynamics optimization. However, I did not see any concrete examples given in the experiments or the discussion. I would suggest that the authors provide a concrete example of why their dataset would be useful for this sort of optimization (this does not have to be an experiment; it can be a fleshed-out theoretical example).

The results for neural networks trained on DrivAerStar look promising. However, how much of a speedup do these approaches give over the state-of-the-art CFD methods? This is important to report so practitioners understand how much of a benefit a neural network-based approach with DrivAerStar can give over state-of-the-art CFD methods.

How did the authors obtain the numbers in Table 1 for DrivAerNet++ and DrivAerML? Did the authors perform the same evaluations with DrivAerNet++ and DrivAerML as they did with the DrivAerStar dataset? I did not see this information reported in the paper (please correct me if I am mistaken), and this is important to know to ensure that the comparison in the table is fair.

I found the role of Star-CCM+ in dataset generation to be unclear; this is important to know if future researchers would like to produce extensions of the DrivAerStar dataset. For example, is Star-CCM+ being used for mesh generation, or are the authors generating a mesh and then feeding it into Star-CCM+ for simulation? I would encourage the authors to explicitly delineate which portions of the dataset generation were performed by Star-CCM+.

Figure 7: The $C_D$ trend line suggests that Transolver underestimates the drag coefficient. Do the authors have intuition for why this is the case?

Figure 7: While the $C_D$ prediction error does decrease from 2.99% to 2.78% when going from 400 to 1200 samples, I don't think this is enough to demonstrate "the dataset’s effective learning scaling properties and potential for further accuracy improvements with additional samples". I would suggest that the author either provide experiments showing a more significant improvement with the number of samples, or that they tone down their claims a bit.

Figure 7: I believe the comprehensive scaling results are in Appendix D.2, not Appendix C.1.

Table A2: What does it mean for the loss to be normalized by the initial condition?

dataset_code_comments.value: While DrivAerStar has 12,000 samples, it appears that only 2,500 samples are publicly available on huggingface. I would encourage the authors to place the entire dataset on huggingface as soon as possible.

summary.value: This paper introduces DrivAerStar, a large-scale, high-fidelity CFD dataset designed to enable industrial-grade machine learning for vehicle aerodynamic optimization. The dataset comprises 12,000 simulations generated using STAR-CCM+, covering three rear body types and 20 CAD parameters via free-form deformation. Each simulation includes detailed aerodynamic data such as surface pressure, velocity fields, and aerodynamic coefficients, all validated against wind tunnel experiments with <1.04% error.

strengths_contributions.value:
i) DrivAerStar provides 12,000 high-fidelity CFD samples generated with STAR-CCM+ and validated against wind tunnel experiments, achieving drag coefficient errors below 1.04%.

ii) The dataset uniquely includes engine bays, cooling channels, and rotating wheels, capturing real-world internal and external flows beyond existing public datasets.

iii) The dataset enables machine learning benchmarks using models like Transolver and PointNet, proving its potential for aerodynamic prediction and efficient surrogate modeling.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
i) The dataset required over 1 million CPU core-hours and 20TB of storage, making it difficult for other researchers to reproduce or scale similar datasets.

ii) Although the dataset includes 20 parameters and 3 rear-end designs, it remains based on the DrivAer platform, which may limit generalization to truly novel vehicle geometries.

title.value: DrivAerStar: An Industrial-Grade CFD Dataset for Vehicle Aerodynamic Optimization

TLDR.value: DrivAerStar introduces a validated dataset of 12,000 industrial-grade CFD simulations for automotive aerodynamics, enabling machine learning models to achieve engineering accuracy while drastically reducing computational costs.

abstract.value: Vehicle aerodynamics optimization has become critical for automotive electrification, where drag reduction directly determines electric vehicle range and energy efficiency. Traditional approaches face an intractable trade-off: computationally expensive Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) simulations requiring weeks per design iteration, or simplified models that sacrifice production-grade accuracy. While machine learning offers transformative potential, existing datasets exhibit fundamental limitations -- inadequate mesh resolution, missing vehicle components, and validation errors exceeding 5% -- preventing deployment in industrial workflows. We present DrivAerStar, comprising 12,000 industrial-grade automotive CFD simulations generated using STAR-CCM+${}^{\textregistered}$ software. The dataset systematically explores three vehicle configurations through 20 Computer Aided Design (CAD) parameters via Free Form Deformation (FFD) algorithms, including complete engine compartments and cooling systems with realistic internal airflow. DrivAerStar achieves wind tunnel validation accuracy below 1.04% -- a five-fold improvement over existing datasets -- through refined mesh strategies with strict wall $y^+$ control. Benchmarks demonstrate that models trained on this data achieve production-ready accuracy while reducing computational costs from weeks to minutes. This represents the first dataset bridging academic machine learning research and industrial CFD practice, establishing a new standard for data-driven aerodynamic optimization in automotive development. Beyond automotive applications, DrivAerStar demonstrates a paradigm for integrating high-fidelity physics simulations with Artificial Intelligence (AI) across engineering disciplines where computational constraints currently limit innovation.
